3._section_summary: This Introduction describes a single study that examines the psychometric properties of the 13-item Body Appreciation Scale (BAS) with Malaysian women and aims to verify its unidimensionality using confirmatory factor analysis. The section also states an aim to examine ethnic differences in body appreciation between Malaysian Chinese and Malay women.

4._section_summary: This section describes the Body Appreciation Scale (BAS; Avalos et al., 2005), a 13-item measure rated on a 5-point scale with higher scores indicating greater body appreciation. It notes that English and German versions show unidimensional structure and validity, and that a Malay version of the BAS was developed using standard back-translation procedures.

5.evidence_source: For the total sample, the mean of all 13 items of the BAS was 3.63 (SD = .72).
5._section_summary: This section reports descriptive statistics for the total sample. Independent samples t-tests showed no significant ethnic differences in participants' age (t(589) = .21, p > .05) and BMI (t(589) = .90, p > .05), and no significant between-group differences in marital status, although religion differed (z = 22.45, p < .001). The mean of all 13 items of the BAS for the total sample was 3.63 (SD = .72).

6.evidence_source: "The hypothesised model included the 13 items of the BAS and a single latent factor on which they were allowed to load."
6._section_summary: This section reports confirmatory and exploratory factor analyses of the 13-item Body Appreciation Scale (BAS) in a single study (total N = 591) that was randomly split into two subsamples (n = 296 and n = 295). A two-factor solution ('General Body Appreciation' and 'Body Image Investment') was retained with adequate fit, and multi-group invariance testing found the two-factor structure to be invariant across Malay (n = 315) and Chinese (n = 276) participants.

7.evidence_source: Between-group differences in BAS Factor Scores We calculated factor scores for each group by taking the mean of responses to items associated with each factor. Results of independent samples t-tests showed no significant differences between Malay and Chinese participants on either of the factor scores: General Body Appreciation (Malay M = 3.63, SD = .86, α = .95; Chinese M = 3.73, SD = .85, α = .95), t(589) = 1.40, p > .05, and; Body Image Investment (Malay M = 3.45, SD = .98, α = .74; Chinese M = 3.46, SD = .97, α = .71), t(589) = 1.01, p > .05.
7._section_summary: This section reports between-group comparisons of BAS factor scores for Malay and Chinese participants using independent samples t-tests. No significant differences were found for General Body Appreciation or Body Image Investment. The section does not provide sample size, country of study, survey method, BMI data, or demographic breakdowns.

8.evidence_source: Participants' BMI was significantly negatively correlated with General Body Appreciation (r = -.24), but did not correlate with Body Image Investment (r = .03) (these correlations take into account measurement error in BAS factors).
8._section_summary: This section reports correlations between BAS factors and BMI. Participants' BMI was significantly negatively correlated with General Body Appreciation (r = -.24) but not with Body Image Investment (r = .03). The negative correlation between BMI and General Body Appreciation remained significant after partialing out age, and age itself was not significantly correlated with either BAS factor.
